title: Improving LLM-based Global Optimization with Search Space Partitioning
claim: Unconstrained LLM sampling collapses onto sparse, degenerate patterns, while partitioning the space yields better coverage and lower set-distance to the domain.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: scatter pair, contour plot, line plot with legend
description: Three-part figure with panels (a), (b) and (c). Panel (a) has two square scatter plots on [0,1]^2. The left one, titled LLM Sampling, shows green dots falling mostly along the diagonal with a few outliers. The right one, titled LLM Partition Sampling, shows red crosses spread evenly across a 4x4 grid of dashed cells. Panel (b) is a purple contour plot of a two-minima function. Orange triangles (global LLM samples) form diagonal streaks, and blue circles (partition samples) cluster in two dashed boxes around the red X minima. Panel (c) is a line chart of Hausdorff distance in 8-D against number of samples, with shaded error bands. Several LLMs plateau high, while Random samples and Gemini 1.5 + partitioning fall to about 0.94. The legend sits below the chart.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as effective surrogate models and candidate generators within global optimization frameworks for expensive blackbox functions. Despite promising results, LLM-based methods often struggle in high-dimensional search spaces or when lacking domain-specific priors, leading to sparse or uninformative suggestions. To overcome these limitations, we propose HOLLM, a novel global optimization algorithm that enhances LLM-driven sampling by partitioning the search space into promising subregions. Each subregion acts as a ``meta-arm'' selected via a bandit-inspired scoring mechanism that effectively balances exploration and exploitation. Within each selected subregion, an LLM then proposes high-quality candidate points, without any explicit domain knowledge. Empirical evaluation on standard optimization benchmarks shows that HOLLM consistently matches or surpasses leading global optimization methods, while substantially outperforming global LLM-based sampling strategies.
